title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the 14th Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en: Special maintenance funds are funds specifically used for the repair, renovation, and upgrading of common parts and common facilities and equipment of a property after the expiration of the warranty period, and are owned collectively by all owners. The payment of special maintenance funds is a statutory obligation that owners must bear to maintain the long-term safe use of the building. Where an owner refuses to pay special maintenance funds and raises a defense based on the statute of limitations, the people's court shall not support such defense.
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Publishing the 14th Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2016] No. 311

To: the High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

Upon deliberation and approval by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the following five cases (Guiding Cases No. 65-69), including the case of the Owners' Assembly of Jiule Building Residential Community in Hongkou District, Shanghai v. Shanghai Huanya Industrial General Corporation — dispute over owners' common ownership rights, are hereby published as the 14th batch of guiding cases for reference in adjudicating similar cases.

September 19, 2016

Guiding Case No. 65

Owners' Assembly of Jiule Building Residential Community in Hongkou District, Shanghai v. Shanghai Huanya Industrial General Corporation — dispute over owners' common ownership rights

(Discussed and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court and published on September 19, 2016)

Keywords: civil; owners' common ownership rights; special maintenance funds; statutory obligation; statute of limitations

Ruling Gist

Special maintenance funds are funds specifically used for the repair, renovation, and upgrading of common parts and common facilities and equipment of a property after the warranty period expires. They belong to all owners in common. Payment of special maintenance funds is a statutory obligation that an owner undertakes to safeguard the long-term safe use of the building. Where an owner refuses to pay special maintenance funds and raises a statute of limitations defense, the people's court shall not support such defense.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 135 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China

Article 79 and Article 83, Paragraph 2 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China

Item 4 of Article 7, Article 54, Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Property Management Regulations

Basic Facts

In March 2004, the defendant, Shanghai Huanya Industrial General Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Huanya Company), acquired title to the ground floor and second floor of Jiule Building in Hongkou District, Shanghai, with a gross floor area of 691.36 square meters for the ground floor and 910.39 square meters for the second floor. Huanya Company did not pay the special maintenance funds for the said premises. In September 2010, the plaintiff, the Owners' Assembly of Jiule Building Residential Community (hereinafter referred to as the Jiule Owners' Assembly), after soliciting the votes of the owners, decided to initiate a lawsuit on behalf of the owners to recover the maintenance funds. The Jiule Owners' Assembly filed a lawsuit with the court, requesting that Huanya Company pay to the plaintiff special maintenance funds of RMB 57,566.9 in respect of the ground floor and second floor premises of Jiule Building owned by it. The defendant, Huanya Company, argued that it had obtained the real property certificate in 2004, and by the time of the lawsuit, six years had passed, and the plaintiff had never demanded the maintenance funds; therefore, the claim had exceeded the statute of limitations, and it opposed the plaintiff's claim.

Judgment

The Hongkou District People's Court of Shanghai rendered civil judgment (2011) Hong Min San (Min) Chu Zi No. 833 on July 21, 2011: the defendant, Huanya Company, shall pay to the plaintiff, the Jiule Owners' Assembly, maintenance funds of RMB 57,566.9 for the ground floor and second floor premises of Jiule Building. After the judgment was pronounced, Huanya Company appealed to the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court. The Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court rendered civil judgment (2011) Hu Er Zhong Min Er (Min) Zhong Zi No. 1908 on September 21, 2011: dismiss the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: Article 79 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Property Law) provides that "maintenance funds for buildings and their ancillary facilities shall be owned by the owners in common. With the joint decision of the owners, they may be used for the repair of common parts such as elevators and water tanks." Article 54, Paragraph 2 of the Property Management Regulations provides that "special maintenance funds belong to the owners and shall be used exclusively for the repair, renovation, and upgrading of common parts and common facilities and equipment of the property after the warranty period expires; they shall not be misappropriated for other purposes." Article 2, Paragraph 2 of the Measures for the Administration of Special Maintenance Funds for Residential Premises (Ministry of Construction and Ministry of Finance Order No. 165) (hereinafter referred to as the Measures) provides that "the special maintenance funds for residential premises as referred to in these Measures mean funds specially used for the repair, renovation, and upgrading of common parts and common facilities and equipment of residential premises after the warranty period expires." According to the above provisions, maintenance funds are by nature special funds, established for a specific purpose, i.e., for the repair, renovation, and upgrading of common parts and common facilities and equipment of residential premises after the warranty period expires. They are raised separately, deposited in separate accounts, and accounted for separately, apart from the purchase price, taxes, and property management fees. Determined by their specific purpose, the payment of special maintenance funds does not arise from a particular transaction or legal relationship but is for the purpose of preparing for emergency repair, renovation, or upgrading of common parts of condominium buildings. Since the maintenance of common parts concerns the common or public interests of all owners, the maintenance funds are public and charitable in nature.

Item 4 of Article 7 of the Property Management Regulations provides that in property management activities, owners shall perform the obligation to pay special maintenance funds in accordance with relevant state provisions. Article 54, Paragraph 1 provides: "Owners of residential premises, non-residential premises within residential communities, or non-residential premises structurally connected to a single residential building shall pay special maintenance funds in accordance with relevant state provisions." According to the above provisions, the payment of special maintenance funds is a statutory obligation specially established for the public interest of a specific scope, i.e., the common interests of all owners of the building. The creation and existence of this obligation depend solely on whether the obligor is an owner of residential or non-residential premises within the scope of a condominium building. Therefore, the obligation to pay special maintenance funds is a statutory obligation aimed at maintaining common or public interests. Only the issue of supplementary payment exists; there is no issue that the obligation can be avoided due to the passage of time.

The right of the owners' assembly to demand supplementary payment of maintenance funds is a managerial right exercised by the owners' assembly on behalf of all owners to fulfill the duty of maintaining the common or public interests of the community. If some owners were allowed to enjoy the benefits brought by the use of maintenance funds paid by other owners to maintain common parts without paying maintenance funds themselves, other owners might pay more than their share for maintaining common parts. This would contravene the principle of fairness and would cause harm to the long-term safe use of the building and to the common or public interests of all owners.

Based on the nature of special maintenance funds and the nature of the owners' obligation to pay them, the defendant, Huanya Company, as an owner of Jiule Building, failed to consciously pay the special maintenance funds in accordance with the law and raised a defense that the owners' assembly's lawsuit for recovery of the special maintenance funds had exceeded the statute of limitations. Such defense cannot be established. The amount calculated by the plaintiff based on the area of the defendant's premises and using the same calculation standard as that used for other owners who paid the special maintenance funds during the same period is reasonable. Therefore, the court ruled that the defendant should pay the special maintenance funds as claimed by the plaintiff.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Lu Weiwei, Chen Wenli, Cheng Min)

Guiding Case No. 66

Lei v. Song — divorce dispute

(Discussed and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court and published on September 19, 2016)

Keywords: civil; divorce; at time of divorce; unauthorized disposition of community property

Ruling Gist

If a party, during the divorce proceedings or before the divorce proceedings, conceals, transfers, sells, or destroys community property, or forges debts in an attempt to encroach upon the other party's property, then when dividing community property upon divorce, the party may be given a lesser share or no share in accordance with Article 47 of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 47 of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, Lei (female), and the defendant, Song (male), registered their marriage on May 19, 2003. Both parties were remarrying and had no children after marriage. Their marital relationship deteriorated due to trivial matters, and they had conflicts in the first half of 2013, and lived separately starting February 2014. Lei previously filed a divorce lawsuit against Song in March 2014, which was dismissed by the court. After that, the relationship between the parties did not improve. In January 2015, Lei filed another lawsuit with the court seeking divorce and equitable division of community property. Song argued that the marital relationship had not broken down and did not agree to the divorce.

Lei claimed that there was community deposit of RMB 370,000 in Song's account with China Postal Savings Bank, and submitted deposit and withdrawal slips and transfer slips as evidence. Song claimed that the RMB 370,000 came from the compensation for demolition of his pre-marital house and his pension, with a remaining balance of approximately RMB 200,000 (including pension of RMB 14,322.48), and submitted account records, judgments, and payment receipts as evidence.

Song claimed that there was community deposit of RMB 250,000 under Lei's name and requested its division. Lei did not acknowledge this. During the first instance trial, she submitted transaction details for account number 4179 (last four digits) with Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) from January 26, 2014, showing a balance of RMB 262.37 as of December 21, 2014. During the second instance proceedings, at Song's request, the court obtained the banking transaction records for Lei's said ICBC account from its opening on November 26, 2012. The records showed that on April 30, 2013, Lei transferred RMB 195,000 from that account to a third party, Lei, via ATM transfer and card withdrawal. Song argued that this deposit was rental income from his pre-marital house and should belong to both parties jointly, and that Lei had transferred community deposits before the divorce. Lei claimed that the deposit was income from the restaurant she operated, initially stating that the money had been used for joint household expenses, and later stating that it was used to repay a loan to her niece, but Lei provided no evidence to support her claims. Additionally, during the trial, Lei had agreed that each party's deposits would belong to themselves and that she would pay an additional RMB 100,000 to Song, but later Lei reneged and refused to pay.

Judgment

The Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing rendered civil judgment (2015) Chao Min Chu Zi No. 04854 on April 16, 2015: grant Lei and Song a divorce; the deposits in Lei's ICBC account ending with 4179 shall belong to Lei; the deposits in Song's China Postal Savings Bank accounts ending with 7101, 9389, and 1156 shall belong to Song; and other issues concerning property and debts were addressed. After the judgment was pronounced, Song appealed, requesting division of the deposits under Lei's name as community property, among other claims. The Beijing Third Intermediate People's Court rendered civil judgment (2015) San Zhong Min Zhong Zi No. 08205 on October 19, 2015: affirm other items of the first instance judgment, reverse item 3 of the first instance judgment, and revise to: the deposits in Lei's ICBC account ending with 4179 shall belong to Lei; the deposits in Song's China Postal Savings Bank accounts ending with 7101, 9389, and 1156 shall belong to Song; and Lei shall pay Song RMB 120,000 within seven days from the date this judgment takes effect.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: The marital relationship is based on the affection between the spouses. During their life together, Song and Lei developed conflicts over trivial matters. After the court rendered a judgment rejecting the divorce petition, the relationship between the parties did not improve. Reconciliation efforts by the court failed. The marital relationship between the parties had indeed broken down, so a divorce should be granted.

The focus of the dispute between the parties in the second instance was whether Lei had transferred community property and how to divide the deposits under the names of both parties. Article 17, Paragraph 2 of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Husband and wife shall have equal right to deal with the property jointly owned by them." Article 47 provides: "If, at the time of divorce, one party conceals, transfers, sells, or destroys the property jointly owned by the couple, or forges debts in an attempt to encroach upon the other party's property, when dividing the property jointly owned by the couple, the party who concealed, transferred, sold, destroyed, or forged debts may be given a smaller share or no share. If, after the divorce, the other party discovers the above acts, the other party may file a lawsuit with the people's court, requesting a new division of the property jointly owned by the couple." This means that if a party, during the divorce proceedings or before the divorce proceedings, conceals, transfers, sells, destroys community property, or forges debts in an attempt to encroach upon the other party's property, such acts infringe upon the other party's equal right to deal with community property. When dividing community property upon divorce, the party who committed such acts shall be given a smaller share or no share in accordance with Article 47 of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China.

In this case, regarding the division of deposits under the names of both parties, based on the relevant evidence, the deposits derived from the compensation for demolition of Song's pre-marital house shall belong to Song individually. The pension obtained by Song after marriage shall be considered community property. The deposits in Lei's ICBC account ending with 4179 were income during the subsistence of the marital relationship and shall be divided as community property. On April 30, 2013, Lei transferred RMB 195,000 from account 4179 to a third party via ATM transfer and card withdrawal. Lei initially stated that the money was used for household expenses, but later stated that it was used to repay an external debt. These statements were clearly contradictory, and she provided no evidence to support her claims, nor could she give a reasonable explanation or account for the disposition of the money. Based on the facts of the case and relevant evidence, it was determined that Lei had the circumstances of transferring and hiding community property. According to the above legal provisions, Lei may receive a smaller share of the deposits in her ICBC account ending with 4179. Song's claim for division of the deposits under Lei's name is in accordance with the law and is supported. Therefore, it was adjudicated that Song's post-marriage pension of RMB 14,322.48 belongs to Song; and for the RMB 195,000 transferred by Lei, Lei shall compensate Song RMB 120,000.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Li Chunxiang, Zhao Xia, Yan Hui)

Guiding Case No. 67

Tang Changlong v. Zhou Shihai — dispute over equity transfer

(Discussed and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court and published on September 19, 2016)

Keywords: civil; equity transfer; installment payment; rescission of contract

Ruling Gist

Where a breach of contract such as delay or non-payment occurs by the transferee of equity in a limited liability company in a transaction where the transfer price is to be paid in installments, and the transferor seeks to rescind the equity transfer agreement entered into between the parties, the provisions of Article 167 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, which allow the seller to rescind the contract when the amount of the purchase price unpaid by the buyer equals one-fifth of the total price, shall not apply.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 94 and Article 167 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

On April 3, 2013, the plaintiff, Tang Changlong, and the defendant, Zhou Shihai, signed an Equity Transfer Agreement and an Equity Transfer Price Payment by Installments Agreement. The parties agreed that Zhou Shihai would transfer to Tang Changlong a 6.35% equity interest in Qingdao Transformer Group Chengdu Shuangxing Electrical Appliance Co., Ltd. The total equity price was RMB 7,100,000, to be paid in four installments: RMB 1,500,000 on April 3, 2013; RMB 1,500,000 on August 2, 2013; RMB 2,000,000 on December 2, 2013; and RMB 2,100,000 on April 2, 2014. The agreement stated that it would take effect upon signature and was irrevocable. After the agreement was signed, Tang Changlong paid the first installment of RMB 1,500,000 to Zhou Shihai on April 3, 2013, as agreed. Because Tang Changlong failed to pay the agreed second installment on time, Zhou Shihai, on October 11 of the same year, served a Notice on Rescission of the Agreement on Tang Changlong by notarization, claiming that Tang Changlong had fundamentally breached the contract and proposing to rescind the Equity Transfer Price Payment by Installments Agreement entered into between the parties. The next day, Tang Changlong transferred the second installment of RMB 1,500,000 to Zhou Shihai and subsequently paid the third and fourth installments in the amounts and at the times agreed. Zhou Shihai, on the grounds that he had already rescinded the contract, returned all four installment payments made by Tang Changlong in full. Tang Changlong then filed a lawsuit with the people's court, requesting a declaration that the notice of rescission issued by Zhou Shihai was invalid and an order that Zhou Shihai continue to perform the contract.

Separately, it was found that on November 7, 2013, in the change (recordation) registration of Qingdao Transformer Group Chengdu Shuangxing Electrical Appliance Co., Ltd., the 6.35% equity interest held by Zhou Shihai had been transferred and recorded in the name of Tang Changlong.

Judgment

The Chengdu Intermediate People's Court of Sichuan Province rendered civil judgment (2013) Cheng Min Chu Zi No. 1815 on April 15, 2014: dismiss the plaintiff Tang Changlong's claims. Tang Changlong, dissatisfied, appealed. The High People's Court of Sichuan Province rendered civil judgment (2014) Chuan Min Zhong Zi No. 432 on December 19, 2014: 1. Set aside the original judgment; 2. Confirm that Zhou Shihai's act of rescinding the Equity Transfer Price Payment by Installments Agreement entered into between the parties is invalid; 3. Tang Changlong shall pay Zhou Shihai the equity transfer price of RMB 7,100,000 within ten days from the date this judgment takes effect. Zhou Shihai, dissatisfied with the judgment of the High People's Court of Sichuan Province, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial on the ground of erroneous application of law by the court of second instance. The Supreme People's Court rendered civil ruling (2015) Min Shen Zi No. 2532 on October 26, 2015, dismissing Zhou Shihai's application for retrial.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: The focus of the dispute in this case is whether Zhou Shihai enjoys the right to rescind the contract under Article 167 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Contract Law).

I. Article 167, Paragraph 1 of the Contract Law provides: "If the amount of the purchase price unpaid by the buyer under an installment sale equals one-fifth of the total price, the seller may demand that the buyer pay the full price or rescind the contract." Paragraph 2 provides: "If the seller rescinds the contract, the seller may demand that the buyer pay a fee for the use of the subject matter." Article 38 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Disputes over Sales Contracts provides: "The term 'installment payment' as used in Article 167, Paragraph 1 of the Contract Law means that the buyer pays the total amount due to the seller in at least three installments over a specified period. If the provisions of an installment sales contract violate Article 167, Paragraph 1 of the Contract Law and harm the interests of the buyer, and the buyer claims that such provisions are invalid, the people's court shall support the claim." According to the above legal provisions and judicial interpretations, the main characteristics of installment sales are: first, the buyer pays the total price to the seller in three or more installments, and the buyer pays the price in two or more installments after the seller delivers the subject matter; second, it is common in transactions between businesses and consumers, usually where the buyer, as a consumer, engages in transactions to meet consumer needs; third, the seller extends some credit to the buyer, and as the credit provider, the seller bears some risk in recovering the price. To guarantee recovery of the remaining price, the seller may exercise the right to rescind the contract under certain conditions.

This case involves the transfer of equity by a shareholder of a limited liability company to a person other than the existing shareholders of the company. Although the form of payment for the equity transfer in this case is also by installments, since the subject matter of the transaction is equity, it differs from general installment sales for consumption purposes in the following characteristics: First, Tang Changlong acquired the equity to participate in the company's management and operations and to obtain economic benefits, not to satisfy personal consumption needs. Second, Zhou Shihai, as the transferor of equity in a limited liability company, bears risks in recovering the equity transfer price by installments that are different from those faced by a seller in a general installment sale for consumption purposes, because the equity he held always exists in the target company. Third, the rescission of the equity transfer contract does not involve a claim for payment for the use of the subject matter against the transferee. In summary, an installment payment contract for equity transfer is significantly different from a general installment sale contract for consumption purposes. Therefore, the right to rescind the contract under Article 167 of the Contract Law should not be simply applied to the "Agreement on Installment Payment of Equity Transfer Price" involved in this case.

II. In this case, the contractual purpose of the parties in entering into the "Agreement on Installment Payment of Equity Transfer Price" can be achieved. The purpose of Tang Changlong and Zhou Shihai in concluding the "Agreement on Installment Payment of Equity Transfer Price" was to transfer Zhou Shihai's 6.35% equity interest in Qingdao Transformer Group Chengdu Shuangxing Electric Appliance Co., Ltd. to Tang Changlong. Based on Tang Changlong's performance of the equity transfer payments, except for the second installment of RMB 1.5 million which was overdue for two months, the remaining three installments were paid as agreed. Zhou Shihai, claiming that Tang Changlong's overdue payment constituted a breach of contract and demanded rescission, returned the RMB 7.1 million paid by Tang Changlong. This does not affect the fact that Tang Changlong will pay the remaining three installments as agreed, and during the proceedings of the first and second instance trials of this case, Tang Changlong clearly expressed his willingness to fulfill the payment obligation. Therefore, the contractual purpose of Zhou Shihai in signing the "Agreement on Installment Payment of Equity Transfer Price" can be achieved. It was also found that on November 7, 2013, in the change (filing) registration of Qingdao Transformer Group Chengdu Shuangxing Electric Appliance Co., Ltd., the 6.35% equity held by Zhou Shihai had been registered and transferred to Tang Changlong's name.

III. From the perspective of good faith, Article 60 of the Contract Law provides that "the parties shall fully perform their obligations as agreed. The parties shall follow the principle of good faith and perform the obligations of notification, assistance, and confidentiality in accordance with the nature, purpose, and trade practices of the contract." Given that the parties explicitly agreed in the equity transfer contract that "this agreement is made in two copies, takes effect upon signature by both parties, and neither party shall renege," even if Zhou Shihai intended to rely on Article 167 of the Contract Law, he should first choose to demand payment of the full price from Tang Changlong, rather than rescind the contract.

IV. From the perspective of maintaining transaction security, an equity transaction in a limited liability company involves many aspects, such as the acceptance and trust of other shareholders in the transferee Tang Changlong (with more than half consenting to the equity transfer), the recording in the register of shareholders, and the registration of equity with the industry and commerce authorities, in which social costs and impacts have already been invested. In this case, after Tang Changlong acquired the equity, he has actually participated in the company's management and operations, and the equity has been registered and transferred to his name. Unless Tang Changlong has a fundamental breach of contract, arbitrarily rescinding the contract may adversely affect the stability of the company's management and operations.

In summary, in this case, Tang Changlong's argument that the basis for Zhou Shihai's demand for rescission of the contract under Article 167 of the Contract Law is insufficient is legally justified and should be supported.

(Judges in the effective judgment: Liang Hongya, Wang Yue, Li Li)

Guiding Case No. 68

Shanghai Ouba Biotechnology Co., Ltd. v. Liaoning Telaiwei Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. — dispute over enterprise loan

(Deliberated and adopted by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on September 19, 2016)

Keywords: civil procedure; enterprise loan; false litigation

Ruling Gist

Where a people's court, in hearing a civil case, discovers the possibility of false litigation, it shall, ex officio, collect relevant evidence, examine the parties in detail, and comprehensively and strictly review whether there are contradictions between the claims and the relevant evidence, and whether the words and actions of the parties during the litigation are inconsistent with common sense. After comprehensive review and judgment, if the parties engage in false civil litigation by fabricating facts, maliciously colluding, evading laws or national policies to seek illegal benefits, the court shall impose sanctions according to law.

Related Legal Provisions

Article 112 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Shanghai Ouba Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Ouba Company) alleged: Ouba Company lent RMB 86.5 million to Liaoning Telaiwei Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Telaiwei Company) for the development of the Telaiwei International Garden real estate project in Donggang City, Liaoning Province. Upon maturity of the loan, Telaiwei Company refused to repay. Therefore, Ouba Company requested the court to order Telaiwei Company to repay the loan principal of RMB 86.5 million and interest.

Telaiwei Company argued: It recognized the facts alleged by Ouba Company in the complaint, stating that all the loan funds had been invested in the Telaiwei International Garden real estate project, and due to sluggish sales of the properties, it was temporarily unable to repay the loan principal and interest.

Xie Tao, the appellant in the first instance, stated: Telaiwei Company and Ouba Company, by fabricating debts, maliciously infringed upon his legitimate rights and interests. He requested the court to ascertain the facts and impose sanctions according to law.

The court found through trial: From July 2007 to March 2009, Ouba Company and Telaiwei Company successively entered into nine Loan Contracts, stipulating that Telaiwei Company would borrow a total of RMB 86.5 million from Ouba Company, with interest set at four times the loan interest rate for the same period in the same year. The loan purpose was limited to the Telaiwei International Garden real estate project. After the loan contracts were signed, Ouba Company remitted a total of 10 sums, amounting to RMB 86.5 million, to Telaiwei Company. However, Telaiwei Company, on the same day or within a few days after receiving the remittances, immediately transferred out 6 of such sums, totaling over RMB 70.5 million. Among these, 5 sums, totaling over RMB 64 million, were transferred to Shanghai Hanhuang Industrial Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hanhuang Company). Additionally, during the period when Ouba Company filed the first instance lawsuit demanding repayment from Telaiwei Company, Ouba Company still remitted 3 sums, totaling RMB 3.6 million, to Telaiwei Company.

The legal representative of Ouba Company was Zong Huiguang. Among its shareholders, Qu Yeli held 73.75% of the equity, Jiang Wenqi held 2%, and Zong Huiguang held 2%. The original legal representative of Telaiwei Company was Wang Zuoxin. Hanhuang Company held 90% of its equity, and Wang Yang held 10%. On August 16, 2010, the legal representative was changed to Jiang Wenqi. The industrial and commercial registration records showed that at the time of the change registration, the signature on the license collection form was by Liu Jingjun, who was also the agent ad litem of Ouba Company during the original first instance trial of this case, and was an employee of Ouba Company. Hanhuang Company was established on March 26, 2002, with Wang Zuoxin as its legal representative, formerly known as Shanghai Telaiwei Cosmetics Co., Ltd. Wang Zuoxin held 67% of its equity, and Qu Yeli held 33%. On October 28 of the same year, Qu Yeli transferred her equity to Wang Yang. On October 10, 2004, the company was renamed Hanhuang Company, and the company registration and related procedures were entrusted to Zong Huiguang. The company was dissolved on July 5, 2011. Wang Zuoxin and Qu Yeli are husband and wife.

During the original first instance trial of this case, on June 22, 2010, Ouba Company applied to the Liaoning High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Liaoning High Court) for property preservation, requesting the seizure, attachment, or freezing of RMB 58.5 million in property of Telaiwei Company. Wang Yang provided two properties in his name, each with a floor area of 236.4 square meters, located at Aomen Road, Heping District, Shenyang City, Liaoning Province, as guarantees for Ouba Company. Wang Zuopeng provided a property in his name with a floor area of 671.76 square meters, located at Ningzhong Road, Huanggu District, Shenyang City, as a guarantee for Ouba Company. Shenyang Shaqi Cosmetics Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shaqi Company, with shareholders Wang Zhenyi and Xiu Guifang) provided two factory buildings in its name, located in Xiao Yangan Village, Baita Town, Dongling District, Shenyang City, with floor areas of 212 square meters and 946 square meters respectively, and a piece of land with a usable area of 4,000 square meters, as guarantees for Ouba Company.

The addresses recorded in the "Application for Opening a Unit Bank Settlement Account" of Ouba Company and Telaiwei Company were both No. 1 Xinxing Road, Donggang City, and the authorized handler for both was Cui Xiufang. During the retrial, Xie Tao provided to the Liaoning High Court a civil judgment (No. (2008) Hu Yi Zhong Min San (Shang) Zhong Zi No. 426) from the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, which was a case of dispute over franchise contracts between Zhang Ezhen and Jia Shike v. Hanhuang Company and Ouba Company. The judgment listed the legal representative of Hanhuang Company as Wang Zuoxin, and the agents ad litem of Ouba Company and Hanhuang Company were both Zong Huiguang, an employee of Hanhuang Company.

Additional facts found during the second instance trial:

(1) Facts concerning the relationship between Ouba Company and Telaiwei Company

Industrial and commercial records show that Shenyang Telaiwei Cosmetics Chain Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shenyang Telaiwei) was established on March 15, 2000. The company was controlled by Ouba Company (holding 96.67% equity), and the handler at the time of establishment was Zong Huiguang. The registered premises were rented from Shenyang Danfei Professional Skin Care Center, whose principal was Wang Zhenyi. On December 23, 2005, Wang Zuoxin, the original legal representative of Telaiwei Company, on behalf of Ouba Company, entered into a chain franchise (licensing) contract with Zhang Ezhen, a person not a party to the case. On February 28, 2007, Huo Jing, on behalf of Telaiwei Company, entered into a "Supplementary Agreement" with Shian Construction Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shian Company) concerning the construction of the Telaiwei International Garden project. In May 2010, Wei Yali, authorized by Telaiwei Company, handled the opening of a bank account, and in September 2011, again on behalf of Ouba Company, handled the opening of a bank account. The contact persons left for both accounts were Wei Yali, with the same telephone number, which was the same as the contact number for Telaiwei Company provided in the civil complaint filed by Ouba Company with the Liaoning High Court on June 10, 2010.

On September 3, 2010, Ouba Company issued a "Reply Letter" to the Liaoning High Court, stating that it agreed to provide a property located at No. 332 Suhong Highway, Qingpu District, Shanghai, with an area of 12,026.91 square meters and a value of RMB 200 million, as security for the preservation measure. Ouba Company acknowledged in court that the aforementioned property was owned by Shanghai Telaiwei Skin Care Products Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shanghai Telaiwei). Shanghai Telaiwei was established on December 9, 2002, with Wang Zuoxin as its legal representative, and shareholders including Wang Zuoxin, Wang Yang (a shareholder of Hanhuang Company), Zou Yan, Zong Huiguang (a shareholder of Ouba Company), Jiang Wenqi, and Wang Qi. Wang Yang also served as a director of Shanghai Telaiwei, Zong Huiguang served as Vice Chairman and Deputy General Manager, Wang Qi served as Deputy General Manager, and Huo Jing served as a director.

On April 20, 2011, Ouba Company applied to the Liaoning High Court for enforcement of the civil judgment (No. (2010) Liao Min Er Chu Zi No. 15), and the court opened a case for enforcement on the same day. On July 12 of the same year, Ouba Company submitted a written application to the Liaoning High Court, stating: "To recover funds as soon as possible and reduce our company's losses, after consultation with the person subject to enforcement, our company allows the person subject to enforcement to sell the remaining properties of this project, provided that our company assigns financial personnel to collect the payments, and all proceeds from the sale of properties must be deposited into the account designated by our company." On September 6, 2011, the Liaoning High Court issued a "Notice of Assistance in Enforcement" to the Donggang Real Estate Management Office, stating that the relevant seized properties had already been delivered to the applicant for enforcement to satisfy the debt, and requested the office to directly register the transfer of the aforementioned properties to the names of third-party purchasers.

After Ouba Company applied for enforcement, besides Xie Tao, other creditors of Telaiwei Company, including Shian Company, Jiangxi Linchuan Construction and Installation Engineering Corporation, and Donggang Qianyang Construction and Installation Engineering Corporation, also submitted objections to enforcement or other forms to the Liaoning High Court, alleging that Ouba Company and Telaiwei Company had fabricated claims to engage in false litigation.

The liquidation committee of Hanhuang Company consisted of Wang Zuoxin, Wang Yang, and Jiang Wenqi, with Wang Zuoxin as the responsible person. The liquidation committee notified all known creditors within 10 days of its establishment and published a cancellation notice in the "Shanghai Commercial Newspaper" on May 14, 2011. On June 25, 2012, Wang Zuoxin transferred equity in Telaiwei Company held by Hanhuang Company: RMB 16 million to Wang Yang, and RMB 2 million to Zou Yan. The industrial and commercial registration was changed on July 9, 2012.

The shareholders of Shaqi Company, Wang Zhenyi and Xiu Guifang, are the father and mother of Wang Zuoxin, respectively. The shareholder Wang Ge of Ouba Company is the daughter of Wang Zuopeng (elder brother of Wang Zuoxin). Wang Zuoxin and Wang Yang are siblings.

(2) Facts concerning fund flows between Ouba Company and the companies involved in the case

The transaction details of Ouba Company's account ending in 8115 (hereinafter referred to as Ouba Company Account 8115) from January 4, 2006, to September 29, 2011, show that starting from March 8, 2006, Ouba Company began to have fund flows with Telaiwei Company. Among them, on March 8, 2006, Ouba Company remitted RMB 3 million from this account to Telaiwei Company's account ending in 4891 (hereinafter referred to as Telaiwei Company Account 4891), with the remark "loan." On June 12, 2006, it transferred RMB 8.01 million to Telaiwei Company. From August 16 to 23, 2007, nearly 70 sums were transferred from Telaiwei Company's account to Ouba Company Account 8115, with the remark mostly "payment for goods." From January 4, 2006, to September 29, 2011, this account had large fund flows with Shaqi Company, Shenyang Telaiwei, Hanhuang Company, and Shanghai Telaiwei, with the remark mostly "payment for goods" or "loan."

The transaction details of Ouba Company's account opened at China Construction Bank, Donggang Sub-branch (ending in 0357) from August 31, 2010, to November 9, 2011, show that on September 15 and September 17, 2010, Ouba Company deposited RMB 1.68 million and RMB 1 million respectively in cash into this account. On September 30, 2010, it paid RMB 1 million as project funds to Donggang Anbang Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. On September 30, 2010, RMB 1 million was transferred from Telaiwei Company's account (ending in 0549) into this account. On August 22, August 30, and September 9, 2011, amounts of RMB 716,985, RMB 514,841, and RMB 623,495 were transferred from Telaiwei Company's account into this Ouba Company account. On November 4, 2011, Telaiwei Company's account ending in 5555 (hereinafter referred to as Telaiwei Company Account 5555) transferred RMB 845,567.87 into this account under the remark "court deduction." On September 27, 2011, RMB 1.935 million was transferred to Ouba Company Account 8115 under the remark "current account payment." On November 9, 2011, RMB 1,579,950 was transferred to Ouba Company's account ending in 4548 (hereinafter referred to as Ouba Company Account 4548).

Records of Ouba Company's account opened at Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Shanghai Qingpu Sub-branch (ending in 5617) show that on July 12, 2012, this account transferred RMB 500,000 to Telaiwei Company under the remark "loan."

Transaction details of Ouba Company's Account 4548 at China Construction Bank, Shenyang Maluwan Sub-branch, from October 7, 2013, to February 7, 2015, show that starting from January 20, 2014, funds transferred from Telaiwei Company into this account under the remark "repayment" were mostly then transferred to Wang Zuopeng's personal account and Shanghai Telaiwei's account under the remark "repayment."

Transaction details of Hanhuang Company's account ending in 4917 at China Construction Bank, Shanghai Branch (hereinafter referred to as Hanhuang Company Account 4917) from January 5, 2006, to January 14, 2009, show that on July 7, 2008, Telaiwei Company Account 4891 transferred RMB 6.05 million into Hanhuang Company Account 4917, and on the same day, Hanhuang Company transferred an equal amount from that account to Telaiwei Company Account 5555. However, the amount transferred from Hanhuang Company to Telaiwei Company's account was counted as part of Telaiwei Company's loan amount, while the amount transferred from Telaiwei Company to Hanhuang Company was not counted as part of Telaiwei Company's repayment amount. During the same period, this account also had fund transfers in and out with Ouba Company and Shaqi Company under the remarks "loan" and "current account payment."

Transaction details of Telaiwei Company Account 5555 from June 7, 2006, to September 21, 2015, show that on July 2, 2009, RMB 6 million was transferred from this account to Ouba Company's account (ending in 0801) under the remark "transfer withdrawal." From November 4, 2011, to December 31, 2014, this account transferred funds to Ouba Company over 30 times, with the largest being a transfer of RMB 18 million to Ouba Company Account 4548 on December 20, 2012. Additionally, this account had multiple large fund transfers to Shaqi Company's account under the remark "loan" from November 13, 2009, to July 19, 2010.

Transaction details of Shaqi Company's account at China Everbright Bank, Shenyang Heping Sub-branch (ending in 6312), from November 13, 2009, to June 27, 2011, show that some of the funds transferred from Telaiwei Company to Shaqi Company were then transferred back to other accounts of Telaiwei Company under the remarks "current account payment" or "loan." For example, on November 13, 2009, RMB 38 million was transferred from Telaiwei Company Account 5555 to Shaqi Company under the remark "loan." On December 4, 2009, RMB 38 million was transferred back to Telaiwei Company's other account ending in 8361 (hereinafter referred to as Telaiwei Company Account 8361) under the remark "current account payment." On February 3, 2010, RMB 48.27 million was transferred from Telaiwei Company Account 8361 to Shaqi Company's account under the remark "current account payment." On February 10 of the same year, RMB 5 million was transferred to Telaiwei Company Account 5555 under the remark "loan," and RMB 19.3 million was transferred to Telaiwei Company Account 4891 under the remark "remittance." On March 31, 2010, Shaqi Company transferred RMB 10 million back to Telaiwei Company Account 8361 under the remark "current account payment." On April 12 of the same year, RMB 18.06 million was transferred back to Telaiwei Company Account 8361 under the remark "intra-system fund transfer." Some of the funds transferred from Telaiwei Company to Shaqi Company's account flowed into Shenyang Telaiwei's account. For example, on May 6, 2010, RMB 10 million was transferred to Shenyang Telaiwei under the remark "loan," and on July 29 of the same year, RMB 22.72 million was transferred to Shenyang Telaiwei under the remark "transfer." Additionally, Ouba Company also transferred some funds into this account under the remark "current account payment."

Both Ouba Company and Telaiwei Company admitted that Ouba Company Account 4548 and its account at China Construction Bank, Donggang Sub-branch (ending in 0357), were controlled by Wang Zuoxin.

Judgment

Liaoning High People's Court rendered a civil judgment (〔2010〕Liao Er Min Chu Zi No. 15) on March 21, 2011, ordering Telewin to repay Ouba the principal of RMB 86.5 million and the interest thereon at the同期 loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China from the date the loan was actually made to the date specified in the judgment for performance. After the judgment became legally effective, Xietao, a person not involved in the case, filed an appeal, and Liaoning High People's Court rendered a civil ruling (〔2012〕Liao Li Er Min Jian Zi No. 8) on January 4, 2012, to retry the case. After retrial, Liaoning High People's Court rendered a civil judgment (〔2012〕Liao Shen Er Min Zai Zi No. 13) on May 20, 2015, dismissing Ouba's claims. Ouba appealed, and the Second Circuit Court of the Supreme People's Court, after trial, rendered a civil judgment (〔2015〕Min Er Zhong Zi No. 324) on October 27, 2015, finding that this case constituted a fictitious civil lawsuit, dismissing the appeal, and affirming the original judgment. At the same time, a decision on fines was issued, imposing fines of RMB 500,000 each on Ouba and Telewin, which participated in the fictitious lawsuit.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The people's court protects lawful lending relationships and, at the same time, shall legally sanction acts of malicious collusion to initiate fictitious lawsuits with the intent to harm the lawful rights and interests of others. There were two issues in dispute in this case: First, whether there was an affiliated relationship between Ouba and Telewin; second, whether there was a genuine lending relationship between Ouba and Telewin regarding the disputed RMB 86.5 million.

I. The issue of whether Ouba and Telewin had an affiliated relationship

Article 217 of the Company Law of the PRC stipulates that an affiliated relationship refers to the relationship between a company's controlling shareholder, actual controller, directors, supervisors, senior management personnel and the enterprises they directly or indirectly control, as well as other relationships that may lead to the transfer of company interests. It can be seen that affiliated companies under the Company Law include both interlocking company shareholders and companies that are directly or indirectly controlled by the same third party, or other relationships between shareholders or between a company's actual controllers, such as direct blood relatives, in-laws, or joint investments, that may lead to the transfer of interests.

In this case, Qu Yeli was the controlling shareholder of Ouba, and Wang Zuoxin was the original legal representative of Telewin and also the controlling shareholder and legal representative of Hanhuang Company, which was the controlling shareholder of Telewin at the time the contracts in question were signed. Wang Zuoxin and Qu Yeli are husband and wife, indicating that Ouba and Telewin were controlled by the couple. Ouba claimed that the two had divorced but did not provide a divorce registration from the civil affairs department or a legally effective court judgment. Although after Liaoning High People's Court accepted the lawsuit in this case, the legal representative of Telewin was changed from Wang Zuoxin to Jiang Wenqi, Wang Zuoxin remained the actual controller of Telewin. At the same time, Zong Huiguang, Wang Qi, and others, who are shareholders and legal representatives of Ouba, jointly invested with Wang Zuoxin, the actual controller of Telewin, Jiang Wenqi, the legal representative of Telewin, and Wang Yang, the current controlling shareholder, to establish Shanghai Telewin, indicating that the shareholders of Ouba and the controlling shareholder and actual controller of Telewin had other common interest relationships. In addition, Shenyang Telewin was a company controlled by Ouba, and the shareholders of Shaqi Company were the parents of Wang Zuoxin. It can be seen that there were affiliated relationships between Ouba and Telewin, and between the aforementioned two companies and Shaqi Company, Shanghai Telewin, and Shenyang Telewin.

There was also a problem of personnel commingling between Ouba and Telewin and other affiliated companies. First, there was commingling among senior management personnel. Jiang Wenqi was both a shareholder and director of Ouba and the legal representative of Telewin, and also participated in the liquidation of Hanhuang Company. Zong Huiguang was both the legal representative of Ouba and an employee of Hanhuang Company. Although Ouba claimed that Zong Huiguang resigned from Hanhuang Company in May 2008, the facts set forth in the civil judgment of the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court (〔2008〕Hu Yi Zhong Min San (Shang) Zhong Zi No. 426) show that during the trial of that case from August to December 2008, Zong Huiguang still participated in the litigation as an employee of Hanhuang Company. Wang Qi was both a supervisor of Ouba and a director of Shanghai Telewin, and also acted as an agent in relevant administrative litigation in the capacity of an employee of that company. Wang Yang was both a supervisor of Telewin and a director of Shanghai Telewin. Wang Zuoxin was the original legal representative and actual controller of Telewin, and also represented Ouba and Hanhuang Company at different times in signing chain franchise (licensing) contracts with third parties not involved in the case. Second, there was also commingling among ordinary employees. Huo Jing was an employee of Ouba, acted as agent for Ouba in the original first-instance litigation of this case, represented Telewin in signing a construction contract with Shi'an Company on February 23, 2007, and simultaneously served as a director of Shanghai Telewin. Cui Xiufang was the accountant of Telewin, opened a bank account for Telewin on January 7, 2010, and after the litigation in this case on August 20, 2010, opened a bank account for Ouba. Ouba stated in court that Wei Yali was an employee of Telewin; in May 2010, Wei Yali was authorized by Telewin to open a bank account, and after the litigation in September 2011, was authorized by Ouba to open a bank account for Ouba at the China Construction Bank Shenyang Maluwan Sub-branch, with Wei Yali listed as the contact person for that bank account. Liu Jingjun was an employee of Ouba, acted as agent for Ouba in the original first-instance and enforcement proceedings of this case, and on March 17, 2009, handled corporate registration and other related matters for Telewin. Liu Yang acted as agent in this case in the capacity of an employee of Telewin, and was also assigned by Wang Zuoxin to act as agent in related litigation for Shanghai Telewin.

The above facts fully demonstrate that there was no strict distinction between the personnel of Ouba, Telewin, and other affiliated companies; the aforementioned personnel actually obeyed the command of Wang Zuoxin alone and, depending on different work tasks, would convert to employees of different affiliated companies at any time. Ouba claimed in its appeal brief that it had dispatched relevant personnel to Telewin at the beginning of the loan in 2007 to supervise the use of the investment funds and assist with work, but Huo Jing had already participated in signing contracts for that company five months before the first loan was allegedly transferred to Telewin by Ouba. Moreover, judging from the role these so-called "dispatched personnel" played in Telewin, they participated in the full range of work, from contract signing and financial management to litigation representation, not just supervision; Ouba's explanation is not credible. Liaoning High People's Court's finding that Ouba and Telewin were affiliated companies controlled by the couple Wang Zuoxin and Qu Yeli was sufficiently supported by evidence.

II. The issue of whether Ouba and Telewin had a genuine lending relationship regarding the disputed RMB 86.5 million

According to Article 90 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the parties shall provide evidence to prove the facts on which their claims are based or the facts used to rebut the other party's claims; if a party fails to provide evidence or the evidence provided is insufficient to prove its factual claims, the party bearing the burden of proof shall bear adverse consequences. Article 108 stipulates: "If the people's court, after examining the evidence provided by the party bearing the burden of proof and considering the relevant facts, is convinced that the existence of the fact to be proven is highly probable, it shall find that the fact exists. If the people's court, after examining the evidence provided by one party to rebut the facts claimed by the party bearing the burden of proof and considering the relevant facts, finds that the existence of the fact to be proven is unclear, it shall find that the fact does not exist." Where an affiliated relationship exists between the parties, to prevent malicious collusion in initiating fictitious lawsuits that harm the lawful rights and interests of others, the people's court must strictly examine whether a genuine lending legal relationship exists.

Ouba filed this lawsuit requesting Telewin to repay RMB 86.5 million in loans and interest. Although it provided loan contracts and transfer vouchers, there were irreconcilable contradictions between its own statements and the evidence it submitted, as well as other evidence in the case. Many of the parties' words and actions before and after the litigation were contrary to common sense, primarily manifested in the following seven aspects:

First, from the perspective of the formation of the loan agreement, the loan contracts may be fictitious. Ouba and Telewin provided unclear statements of the details of the offer and acceptance of the loan legal relationship, especially Zong Huiguang, Ouba's legal representative who claimed to be the contract handler, who provided vague details regarding the time, place, and the handlers for each party of all loan contracts. Each loan in question was for a large amount, yet the parties provided unclear statements of the details, or even general circumstances, of the signing of all contracts, which is unreasonable.

Second, from the perspective of the timing of the loans, the evidence submitted by the parties was contradictory. Ouba's statements and the loan contracts it submitted indicate that Ouba began its loan relationship with Telewin in July 2007. However, after appealing to this court, the audit report commissioned by Ouba itself stated that loans to Telewin began in December 2006. Yet, based on the bank account transaction details of Telewin and Ouba, before December 2006, there were already two transfers totaling up to RMB 11 million from Ouba's account 8115, including a transfer of RMB 3 million under the name "loan" to Telewin's account on March 8, 2006, and a transfer of RMB 8.01 million on June 12 of the same year.

Third, from the perspective of the amount of the loans, the parties' claims were contradictory. After filing the lawsuit, Ouba first claimed that the cumulative loan amount since July 2007 was RMB 58.5 million, then changed it to RMB 86.5 million during the litigation, and further claimed the total loan amount was RMB 108.5 million on appeal. The claimed loan amount changed several times, but only loan contracts for RMB 86.5 million were provided. Moreover, the bank transfer vouchers submitted by Xietao in court showed that, in addition to the alleged RMB 108.5 million loan, there were more than RMB 44 million in funds transferred into Telewin's account under the name "loan." Ouba admitted that these additional amounts were transfers made at Wang Zuoxin's request to help with transfers and were not genuine loans. This admission shows that Ouba filled in the purpose of the funds on the relevant bank vouchers extremely arbitrarily. According to the amounts shown in the bank account transaction details obtained by this court, the amount of funds transferred into Telewin's account by Ouba under the name "loan" far exceeded the amounts successively claimed by Ouba. In addition, there were other multiple transfers of huge sums under the name "loan" into Telewin's account that were not included in the scope of the loan amount claimed by Ouba.

Fourth, from the perspective of the flow of funds, Ouba unilaterally counted the outflow from its own account while ignoring the inflow. Whether during the loan period specified in the loan contracts, before that period, or even after the litigation began, the fund flows between the accounts of Ouba and Telewin included both transfers from Ouba to Telewin's account and transfers from Telewin to Ouba's account. However, Ouba only calculated the debit amount transferred out of its own account and made no mention of the credit amount transferred in from Telewin.

Fifth, from the perspective of transfers among all affiliated companies, there was circular transfer of funds between two or more parties. As mentioned above, comparing the accounts among Ouba, Telewin, Hanhuang Company, and Shaqi Company, there was a phenomenon where Telewin transferred its own funds to Hanhuang Company's account, which then flowed through Ouba's account, and subsequently returned to Telewin's account, resulting in artificially inflated loans. Such a situation also existed in fund flows between Telewin and other affiliated companies.

Sixth, from the perspective of the purpose of the loans, it contradicted the contract terms. Article 2 of the loan contracts stipulated that the loans were limited to use for the Telwein International Garden real estate project. However, after the funds in question were transferred into Telewin's account, Telewin immediately transferred most of the funds to Hanhuang Company and Shaqi Company under the names "loan" and "repayment," which ultimately flowed back to Ouba and Ouba's controlled company, Shenyang Telewin. As for Ouba's argument that Telewin transferred funds to Hanhuang Company to repay loans owed to Hanhuang Company, because the loan amounts between Hanhuang Company and Telewin provided by Ouba contradicted the actual transaction amounts in the bank accounts of the two companies, and most of the funds flowed back to Ouba or its controlled companies, Ouba's argument is unfounded.

Seventh, from the perspective of the conduct of Ouba, Telewin, and their affiliated companies during the litigation and enforcement, it was contrary to everyday experience. After Ouba filed the lawsuit, it continued to transfer funds with Telewin; Telewin continuously transferred huge sums into Ouba's account, but during the litigation and enforcement proceedings, it did not raise any defense against Ouba's claim regarding the repayment amount; Ouba applied to Liaoning High People's Court for property preservation, and Wang Yang, a shareholder of Telewin, provided his own real property as security for Ouba, which should have been an opposing party; the ownership of the real property in Qingpu District, Shanghai, which Ouba additionally provided as security in the original first-instance litigation, actually belonged to Shanghai Telewin, whose legal representative was Wang Zuoxin; Ouba and Telewin admitted in court that the bank accounts Ouba opened at China Construction Bank Donggang Sub-branch and China Construction Bank Shenyang Maluwan Sub-branch were both controlled by Wang Zuoxin.

Ouba and Telewin failed to provide reasonable explanations for the above contradictions and circumstances contrary to common sense. It can be seen that Ouba did not provide sufficient evidence to prove the existence of a genuine lending relationship with Telewin regarding the disputed funds. Moreover, from the transaction details of the accounts of Ouba, Telewin, and their affiliated companies obtained, it was found that there were arbitrary transfers between Ouba, Telewin, and other affiliated companies, and between different accounts of the same company, with the purpose of the funds filled in arbitrarily. Combined with other evidence in the case, the court was convinced that the creditor's right claimed by Ouba was fabricated by intercepting the fund flows between Ouba and Telewin, and its request for Telewin to repay RMB 86.5 million in loans and interest based on the fabricated creditor's right should not be supported. Accordingly, Liaoning High People's Court's judgment in the retrial dismissing Ouba's claims was not improper.

As to whether Ouba and Telewin initiated this lawsuit with malicious collusion to harm the lawful rights and interests of others. First, both Ouba and Telewin were aware of the creditor-debtor relationships between Telewin and the first-instance appellant Xietao and other creditors. From the enforcement process of the judgment in this case, after Ouba applied for enforcement, it did not agree to the court's auction of the sealed-up real property but continued to allow Telewin to sell it. Each time Telewin sold a unit, Ouba would apply to the court to lift the seal on that unit. When questioned in court, Ouba could not clearly state how many sealed properties Telewin had sold or how much debt had been repaid, indicating that it initiated this lawsuit not to realize its creditor's rights but to use judicial procedures for protective sealing to prevent other creditors from being satisfied from Telewin's assets. The purpose of fabricating creditor's rights, maliciously colluding, and harming others' lawful rights and interests was obvious. Second, from the facts of personnel commingling between Ouba and Telewin and their bank accounts being jointly controlled by Wang Zuoxin, it can be seen that the two companies were under the same control and had lost the independent legal personality that a corporate legal person should possess. Article 112 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC provides: "If parties maliciously collude and attempt to harm the lawful rights and interests of others through litigation, mediation, or other means, the people's court shall dismiss their request and, depending on the severity of the circumstances, impose fines or detention; if a crime is constituted, criminal liability shall be investigated according to law." The opinion of the first-instance appellant, Xietao, that Ouba and Telewin maliciously colluded to initiate a fictitious lawsuit harming his lawful rights and interests, and his request for sanctions against the relevant parties and responsible persons, are legally based and should be supported.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Hu Yunteng, Fan Xiangyang, Wang Guoxian)

Guiding Case No. 69

Wang Mingde v. Leshan Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security — dispute over work-related injury recognition

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on September 19, 2016)

Keywords
administrative litigation/work-related injury recognition/procedural administrative act/acceptance

Ruling Gist

If a party believes that a procedural administrative act taken by an administrative organ infringes upon its lawful rights and interests such as personal rights or property rights, has a clear and actual impact on its rights and obligations, and cannot obtain relief through filing a lawsuit against the relevant substantive administrative act, and files an administrative lawsuit against the procedural administrative act, the people's court shall accept the case in accordance with the law.

Related Legal Provisions

Article 12, Article 13 of the Administrative Litigation Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, Wang Mingde, is the father of Wang Leibing. Wang Leibing was an employee of the Emeishan Branch of Sichuan Jiabao Asset Management Group Co., Ltd. On March 18, 2013, Wang Leibing died in a traffic accident. Because the cause of Wang Leibing's motorcycle falling and overturning could not be ascertained, the Traffic Police Brigade of the Emeishan City Public Security Bureau of Sichuan Province issued a Road Traffic Accident Certificate (No. Le Gong Jiao Ren Ding 〔2013〕 No. 00035) on April 1 of the same year in accordance with Article 50 of the Regulations on Procedures for Handling Road Traffic Accidents. The Road Traffic Accident Certificate stated: On March 18, 2013, Wang Leibing was driving an unlicensed "Kadiwang" two-wheeled motorcycle from the large roundabout to the small roundabout in Emeishan City. At approximately 1:20 a.m., when the vehicle reached 29.3 km of Provincial Road S306, it drove to the right side of the road, scraped against the edge of the median strip, and overturned into the median strip, resulting in vehicle damage and Wang Leibing's immediate death.

On April 10, 2013, the third party, the Emeishan Branch of Sichuan Jiabao Asset Management Group Co., Ltd., applied to the defendant, Leshan Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security, for work-related injury recognition for its employee Wang Leibing's death in the traffic accident, and simultaneously submitted evidence including the Road Traffic Accident Certificate issued by the Traffic Police Brigade of Emeishan City Public Security Bureau. The defendant, on the grounds that the traffic management department of the public security organ had not yet issued a traffic accident determination document for the accident in this case, issued a Notice of Suspension of Time Limit for Work-Related Injury Recognition (No. Le Ren She Gong Shi 〔2013〕 No. 05 (Emeishan City)) (hereinafter "Suspension Notice") on the same day, and served it on the plaintiff and the third party.

On June 24, 2013, the plaintiff submitted a "Application to Resume Work-Related Injury Recognition" to the defendant via domestic express mail, requesting the defendant to resume the work-related injury recognition for Wang Leibing. Because the defendant did not resume the work-related injury recognition procedure for Wang Leibing, the plaintiff filed an administrative lawsuit with the court on July 30 of the same year, requesting a judgment to revoke the Suspension Notice issued by the defendant.

Judgment

The Central District People's Court of Leshan, Sichuan Province, rendered judgment on September 25, 2013, in Case No. (2013) Lezhong Xing Chu Zi No. 36, revoking the "Notice of Suspension" (Leshangongshigongshi [2013] No. 05) issued by the defendant, Leshan Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security, on April 10, 2013. After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, Leshan Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security filed an appeal. During the second-instance trial before the Leshan Intermediate People's Court, Leshan Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security submitted an application for withdrawal of appeal. Upon review, the Leshan Intermediate People's Court held that the appellant's voluntary application for withdrawal of appeal represented its true intention and complied with legal provisions, and therefore ruled to permit the withdrawal of the appeal by Leshan Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security. The first-instance judgment has taken legal effect.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that there were two issues in dispute: first, whether the "Notice of Suspension" was an actionable administrative act; second, whether the "Notice of Suspension" should be revoked.

I. Whether the "Notice of Suspension" is an actionable administrative act

The court held that the defendant's issuance of the "Notice of Suspension" constituted a procedural administrative act within the process of determining work-related injury. If such an act does not involve a final determination and has no substantive impact on the rights and obligations of the counterparty, it is an immature administrative act and is not actionable. If the counterparty initiates administrative litigation, it does not fall within the scope of cases accepted by the people's court. However, if such a procedural administrative act is final, has a substantive impact on the rights and obligations of the counterparty, and the counterparty cannot obtain relief through litigation against the relevant substantive administrative act, then it is an actionable administrative act, and administrative litigation initiated by the counterparty falls within the scope of administrative cases accepted by the people's court.

Although Article 73 of the Road Traffic Safety Law of the PRC provides: "The traffic management department of the public security organ shall, based on the on-site inspection, examination, investigation, and relevant inspection and appraisal conclusions of the road traffic accident, promptly produce a written determination of the road traffic accident as evidence for handling the accident. The written determination of the road traffic accident shall state the basic facts, causes, and responsibilities of the parties involved in the road traffic accident and shall be served on the parties," in actual road traffic accidents, there are also situations where the causes of the accident cannot be ascertained and the traffic management department of the public security organ cannot produce a written determination of the road traffic accident. In this regard, Article 50 of the Provisions on Procedures for Handling Road Traffic Accidents provides: "If the cause of a road traffic accident cannot be ascertained, the traffic management department of the public security organ shall issue a certificate of road traffic accident, stating the time, place, information of the parties, and the facts obtained through investigation, and shall serve the certificate on each party separately." In the present case, the Traffic Police Brigade of the Emeishan Public Security Bureau, based on the accident circumstances it investigated regarding Wang Leibing's death in a traffic accident, could only legally issue a "Certificate of Road Traffic Accident" and was unable to produce a "Written Determination of Road Traffic Accident." Therefore, the "Certificate of Road Traffic Accident" in this case was already the conclusion reached by the traffic management department of the public security organ in accordance with the Provisions on Procedures for Handling Road Traffic Accidents, namely the "conclusion of a judicial organ or relevant competent administrative department" required for the determination of work-related injury under Article 20, paragraph 3, of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance. Unless new facts or statutory reasons arose, the traffic management department of the public security organ would not produce any other conclusion regarding the traffic accident involved in this case. Moreover, the defendant, when the third party applied for a determination of work-related injury, had already submitted the relevant "Certificate of Road Traffic Accident," yet still issued the "Notice of Suspension." Furthermore, until the date the plaintiff filed the lawsuit, the defendant continued to refuse to resume the process of determining whether Wang Leibing's death constituted a work-related injury, on the ground that the work-related injury determination was suspended. It can thus be seen that although the defendant's issuance of the "Notice of Suspension" was a procedural act in the determination of work-related injury, this act would cause the plaintiff's lawful rights and interests to be deprived of legal remedy for a long period, even permanently, directly affecting the plaintiff's lawful rights and interests and producing a substantive impact on their rights and obligations. Moreover, the plaintiff could not obtain relief by filing a lawsuit against the relevant substantive administrative act. Therefore, the defendant's issuance of the "Notice of Suspension" constituted an actionable administrative act, and the people's court should accept the case in accordance with the law.

II. Whether the "Notice of Suspension" should be revoked

The court held that Article 20, paragraph 3, of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance provides: "If the determination of work-related injury requires a conclusion from a judicial organ or relevant competent administrative department as a basis, the time limit for making the determination of work-related injury shall be suspended while the judicial organ or relevant competent administrative department has not yet reached a conclusion." As previously discussed, the third party had already submitted the "Certificate of Road Traffic Accident" when applying to the defendant for a determination of work-related injury regarding Wang Leibing's death. In other words, when the third party applied for the work-related injury determination, there was no circumstance as provided in Article 20, paragraph 3, of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance that would legally justify a decision to suspend. Therefore, the defendant's issuance of the "Notice of Suspension" pursuant to Article 20 of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance constituted an error in the application of laws and regulations and should be revoked. Additionally, it should be pointed out that after the judgment revoking the defendant's "Notice of Suspension" takes legal effect, the defendant's process for determining whether the employee in question had suffered a work-related injury should be resumed.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Huang Ying, Li Ju, Peng Dong)
